power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

info.title: Does Early Childhood Education and Care for Infants and Toddlers Cause Behavior Problems Up to Age 8?

								University of Oslo
								
									Eric

text.text: Background: The causal effect of attending Early Childhood Education and Care (ECEC) for infants and toddlers on child behavior problems is contested.
Yet, most previous research is correlational.
Findings from previous research are mixed, but with some evidence of harmful effects on children's behavior.
Some correlational studies also suggest that ECEC may be most harmful for children from socioeconomically advantaged families.

Methods: We estimate the effect of age of entry into ECEC on externalizing behavior problems at ages 3, 5, and 8 years in a large sample (n=66,394) from The Norwegian Mother, Father, and Child Cohort study (MoBa).

We use two quasi-experimental methods, Two-Way Fixed-Effects models and Instrumental Variable models, that exploit variations in how early families enrolled their children in ECEC due to a national scale-up of publicly funded centers.

Results: In this high-powered, rigorous approach to testing the causal impact of age of entry into ECEC, we find no evidence that entry around age 1 relative to later affects behavior problems either during preschool years (at ages 3 or 5) or after school entry (at age 8 years).
We also find no evidence that these effects vary by parental education or family income.
We find no evidence suggesting that early entry into ECEC has harmful consequences for children's behavior regulation, during the preschool years or after school entry.
We argue that our null results may be due to ECEC pedagogy in Norway that emphasizes young children's well-being and playful learning experiences.

There are long-standing concerns about the harmful effects of early, extensive, and continuous non-parental care on children's behavior regulation, especially center-based Early Childhood Education and Care-ECEC (Belsky, 2001; Huston, Bobbitt, & Bentley, 2015).
text.formatted: There are long-standing concerns about the harmful effects of early, extensive, and continuous non-parental care on children's behavior regulation, especially center-based Early Childhood Education and Care-ECEC <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(Belsky, 2001;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">Huston, Bobbitt, & Bentley, 2015)</ref>.

text.text: These concerns appear reasonable in light of several correlational studies, most prominently based on U.S. data from the NICHD Study of Early Child Care and Youth Development (SECCYD).

text.text: In these data, there were no associations between the total amount of care and behavior problems when children were 3 years old, but the associations appeared at age 4½ years (NICHD Early Child Care Research Network, 2003) and continued through age 15 (Vandell, Belsky, Burchinal, Steinberg, & Vandergrift, 2010; see also review by Huston, et al., 2015).
text.formatted: In these data, there were no associations between the total amount of care and behavior problems when children were 3 years old, but the associations appeared at age 4½ years <ref type="bibr">(NICHD Early Child Care Research Network, 2003)</ref> and continued through age 15 <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">(Vandell, Belsky, Burchinal, Steinberg, & Vandergrift, 2010</ref>; see also review by <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">Huston, et al., 2015)</ref>.

text.text: Taken together, researchers have argued that starting ECEC early and spending more time in care across the early childhood years may disrupt behavioral development.
However, results from correlational studies like these may be biased by unobserved confounding variables and are therefore not credible for causal inference.

A review of quasi-experimental studies-with credible causal identification-found inconsistent support for the hypothesis that ECEC quantity (defined variously as age of entry, hours per week, and attending vs. not) has adverse effects on behavior problems during the preschool years (Dearing & Zachrisson, 2017).

text.text: More recently, harmonized within-person change analyses of seven datasets from five countries found no evidence that more hours per week in ECEC caused behavior problems during the preschool years (Rey-Guerra et al., 2023).

text.text: Yet, several studies do report harmful effects.
In France, short-term negative effects of ECEC use in the first year of life were evident at age 2 in a quasi-experimental study (Berger, Panico, & Solaz, 2021).
text.formatted: In France, short-term negative effects of ECEC use in the first year of life were evident at age 2 in a quasi-experimental study <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(Berger, Panico, & Solaz, 2021)</ref>.

text.text: Moreover, although correlational longitudinal studies in Quebec, studying amount of time spent in care, did not find harmful effects (Orri et al., 2019; Pingault et al., 2015), a quasi-experimental evaluation of a policy reform in Canada (Quebec) found both short-and long-term harmful effects of a rollout of subsidized slots (Baker, Gruber, & Milligan, 2008; Baker, Gruber, & Milligan, 2019).

text.text: In addition, reports from the randomized Tennessee Preschool program have reinvigorated concerns about harmful effects of attending ECEC for preschool aged children.

Specifically, while the short-term effects on behavior problems from this RCT initially were small and insignificant, they grew larger and became statistically significant during the elementary schooling years, suggesting a sleeper effect in which a causal effect that is at first undetectable later becomes evident (Durkin, Lipsey, Farran, & Wiesen, 2022; Lipsey, Farran, & Durkin, 2018).

text.text: In this study, we test whether there are adverse effects of ECEC for infants and toddlers on behavior problems through early school age in Norway.

Specifically, we tested for causal effects of age of entry (from age one) into ECEC on externalizing behavior problems during the preschool years (ages 3 and 5) and at age 8, two to three years after school entry (which in Norway happens in August, the year the child turns six).
We also tested whether these effects differed as a function of parental education and income.

Previous correlational research has shown socioeconomic gradients in associations between both age of entry into, and intensity of, ECEC on behavior problems. Huston et al.'s (2015) review suggests that harmful effects across child ages are concentrated among children from higher socioeconomic status (SES) households, while Orri et al. (2019) found that attending ECEC prevents later behavior problems among children from lower SES families, yet with no associations for others.
text.formatted: Previous correlational research has shown socioeconomic gradients in associations between both age of entry into, and intensity of, ECEC on behavior problems. <ref type="bibr">Huston et al.'s (2015)</ref> review suggests that harmful effects across child ages are concentrated among children from higher socioeconomic status (SES) households, while <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">Orri et al. (2019)</ref> found that attending ECEC prevents later behavior problems among children from lower SES families, yet with no associations for others.

text.text: Norway is a particularly relevant context for testing adverse effects of age of entry into ECEC for multiple reasons.
First, a policy reform in Norway during the 2000s led to a sharp increase in the availability of ECEC for one-and two-year-old children.
The reform led to a vast majority (nearly 80%) of infants and toddlers entering ECEC in their second year of life (and remaining there on a full-day basis until school entry age).
Therefore, many children are exposed to early, extensive, and continuous care in Norway.
Yet, the Norwegian ECEC context is characterized by a holistic focus on child well-being rather than a strong focus on school readiness, which is common in many other countries.
Theory suggests that an earlier age of entry into early education should be the most harmful because of early separation from attachment figures (Belsky, 2001).
text.formatted: Theory suggests that an earlier age of entry into early education should be the most harmful because of early separation from attachment figures <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(Belsky, 2001)</ref>.

text.text: Whether this applies regardless of context is uncertain.
Second, Norway provides a unique opportunity for a quasi-experimental design to test the longer-term effects of ECEC.
Specifically, the policy reform caused the national coverage rate of infant and toddler ECEC to rise from 38% to 77% through the 2000s.
(For details on the ECEC expansion, see Online Appendix 1.)

The policy expansion coincided by serendipity with the rollout of a multi-cohort longitudinal study, the Norwegian Mother, Father, and Child Cohort Study, which collected data on children and their families on multiple occasions, including behavior problems.

This unique combination of a policy reform and survey data allowed us to test the effects of age of entry into ECEC on behavior problems using two analytical approaches: Two-Way Fixed-Effects regression models and Instrumental Variable models.

Finally, there is evidence that the scale-up of ECEC in Norway had positive effects on achievement outcomes up to age 15 for children from families where parents had low levels of education, but null-effects for others (Almås, Drange, Meghir, & Zachrisson, 2026; Zachrisson, Dearing, Borgen, Sandsør, & Karoly, 2024).
text.formatted: Finally, there is evidence that the scale-up of ECEC in Norway had positive effects on achievement outcomes up to age 15 for children from families where parents had low levels of education, but null-effects for others <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(Almås, Drange, Meghir, & Zachrisson, 2026;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">Zachrisson, Dearing, Borgen, Sandsør, & Karoly, 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Knowing whether a reform with positive effects for a subgroup also has negative effects is important.

Other studies from Norway not exploiting the reform have found that while an earlier age of entry into ECEC (starting at about one year of age) caused slightly elevated levels of child aggression at age 2, these effects had faded by age 4 (Dearing et al., 2015).

text.text: Also, hours per week in ECEC (from age 1 ½ to 3 years) have been found to be unrelated to behavior problems once unobserved confounding was accounted for in the research design (Zachrisson et al., 2013), which was replicated up to age 4 in a different sample (Rey-Guerra et al., 2023).

text.text: We used two approaches to estimating the effects of age of entry into ECEC on measures of behavior problems at child ages 3, 5, and 8 (i.e., 2 nd /3 rd grade): Two-Way Fixed-Effects (FE) regression models and instrumental variable (IV) regressions.
Extensive descriptions of statistical analyses are in Online Appendix 3.

The FE model compares children living in the same municipality and belonging to the same cohort who start ECEC at different ages, using the full variation in age of entry into ECEC to estimate the average treatment effect.
This model provides efficient (i.e., precise) estimates.

However, while the FE model controls for unobserved variability between municipalities, and our comprehensive set of covariates (e.g., household income, maternal depression, and birth weight) addresses concerns related to within-municipality sorting, we cannot fully rule out the possibility that children who start ECEC early may differ from those who start later.

To provide more robust causal estimates, the IV model uses variation in age of entry into ECEC caused by the policy expansion to estimate the local average treatment effect (LATE) for those induced to start earlier because of the policy.

Using only the variability in age of entry induced by the available slots leads to less precise estimates relative to the FE models, highlighting a common trade-off between estimation efficiency and risk of bias.
Additionally, because LATE identifies effects for those affected by the policy, the estimates cannot be directly compared to the ECEC effects estimated by the FE model.
The IV model relies on assumptions about instrument relevance, independence, and exclusion.
We describe these IV assumptions thoroughly in Appendix 3, along with empirical validation efforts.

As a preliminary step, we probed the functional form (i.e., linear versus non-linear) of the association between age of entry into ECEC and externalizing problems and found little evidence of non-linearity (see online Appendix 5).
Thus, in our primary models, we employ linear estimators.

text.text: When discussing null-findings, it is important to acknowledge that absence of evidence is not evidence of absence.
The logic of null-hypothesis testing allows us to fail to reject a hypothesis, but not to prove the null hypothesis (Schuengel, 2022).
text.formatted: The logic of null-hypothesis testing allows us to fail to reject a hypothesis, but not to prove the null hypothesis <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">(Schuengel, 2022)</ref>.

text.text: Interpreting our results therefore requires us to state what magnitude of effect we would regard as substantively meaningful, independently of statistical significance.

We adopt two benchmarks estimated in the same sample and on the same measures as our treatment effects: the raw gender difference in externalizing behavior, which was 12.6%, 24.0% and 12.1% of an SD at ages 3, 5 and 8; and the difference between children whose parents both had less than high school and children whose parents both held a long university degree, which was 40.0%, 49.3% and 18.0% of an SD.
Both are differences this literature routinely treats as consequential.

Following Schuengel (2022), we then applied equivalence tests, which ask whether the hypothesis of a meaningful effect can be rejected against a declared smallest effect size of interest in both the positive and negative direction (implemented as two onesided tests).
Our IV estimates are equivalent to zero at a threshold of 0.20 SD at all three ages, the smallest thresholds at which equivalence holds being 0.16, 0.18 and 0.16 of an SD at ages 3, 5 and 8.

Set against our benchmarks, the IV estimates thus exclude harmful effects as large as the difference associated with parental education at every age, and as large as the gender difference at age 5; at ages 3 and 8, where the gender difference is smaller, the equivalence bound approaches but does not fall below it.

Our fixed-effects estimates, which are considerably more precise but rest on a selection-on-observables assumption within municipality and cohort, point to the same conclusion and are equivalent to zero at a threshold of 0.02 SD.
While smaller effects cannot be ruled out, we therefore read these results as evidence against harmful effects of early, extensive, and continuous ECEC.

Our data are unique because we leverage a population-wide longitudinal health survey (MoBa) in combination with registry data, providing detailed information on behavior problems across time and family-level covariates, with the rollout of the survey coinciding with a large policy expansion.
This allows us to use two strong research designs, FE and IV, to probe the harmful effects of early age of entry into ECEC.
Each design offers considerable advantages compared to traditional designs, where accounting for selection into care relies solely on observed covariates.
Yet, because they are both based on distinct sets of assumptions, our results are considerably strengthened by the consistent patterns observed across these complementary designs.
The designs used in this paper have different strengths and weaknesses and provide estimates with different interpretations.

In summary, we believe our strong research designs with distinct non-overlapping assumptions provide support for the lack of evidence for harmful effects of ECEC for infants and toddlers in Norway, well into school age.

These findings are consistent with, and extend, previous quasi-experimental studies investigating potentially harmful short-term effects of ECEC in Norway, including age of entry (Dearing et al., 2015) and hours in care (Zachrisson et al., 2013).

text.text: This discrepancy may indicate between-country differences in the quality and content of the ECEC services and wider family policies.

Lack of evidence for harmful effects of ECEC in Norway may be explained by the care and pedagogical approach of ECEC in Norway, which is less focused on school readiness and academic skill learning than in other contexts like, e.g., North America.

Specifically, in Norway, ECEC policy and practice standards place a major emphasis on a holistic approach to early childhood development in which free play, child-initiated activities, and child well-being are central elements, and formal instruction is virtually absent (OECD, 2015).

text.text: This contrasts with contexts where teacher-led instructions and formal learning are more strongly emphasized and may be more facilitating for development of behavioral regulation.

For example, in the US, while the Tennessee Preschool Program met most national recommendations for content of the program, those recommendations put emphasis on formal group instruction, akin to a school setting (Lipsey et al., 2018).

text.text: Specifically, they argue that an alignment between the pedagogy guiding the environment in ECEC and the children's developmental needs is crucial for providing an enriching environment.
Moreover, structural quality in Norway is highly regulated and homogeneous across settings.

This includes staff-child ratios of 1:3 for one-and two-year olds and 1:6 for older children; a national curriculum (framework plan) guiding the pedagogical content; and regulations for indoor and outdoor spaces.

text.text: As the current evidence on the reform suggests benefits for cognitive and achievement outcomes, while suggesting no apparent effects on behavior, it may be reasonable to speculate that the child-centered and holistic approach of the Norwegian ECEC system is overall beneficial.
While our study has considerable strengths in numbers and design, there are notable limitations.
First of all, although MoBa is population-wide, it had a relatively low participation rate (41%) and considerable attrition.
Children of non-Norwegian background are especially underrepresented, as are children from families with less money and less parental education.

While Zachrisson et al. (2024) showed that associations between socioeconomic indicators and achievement test scores were similar in families attending MoBa and in the general population, we have no guarantee that this is true for behavior problems, or that the treatment effect of ECEC is identical in the two groups.

text.text: In conclusion, our analyses of large, population-wide data using strong quasiexperimental methods do not provide evidence supporting harmful effects related to age of entry into ECEC in Norway, up to third grade.
We therefore argue that potentially harmful effects should be interpreted in light of the content and quality of the ECEC environment children attend.
Early entry into ECEC is not universally harmful.
